sections.heading:
40 CYCLES BEFORE THE UNFOLDING 
 VIVIFLUX MODULE ONE · YREUS STATION
paragraphs: General Dennis Reed pressed close to the observation glass. The cold seeped through the pane. On the other side of it, Subject N. V. returned his gaze with sad milky eyes. He'd been reviewing case files for clicks. He had tried, at first, to keep her human designation intact. But now he simply called her Envee. Still, he couldn't prepare himself for the moment she looked back. His breath hitched.

She sat naked on a block of basalt. Bald. No eyebrows. Her skin had the matte gray of volcanic ash. A tremor rattled Dennis' fingers as he checked the readout. The frost on the inner glass had grown fractals overnight.
Temperature: minus 54°C, steady.
A human could not have lasted one thud in there. She'd been in the box for six.
*But she's not human anymore,* Dennis thought.

paragraphs.text: "Ready?" he asked.
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs.text: "Cellular transition nominal," said a CIX from the station behind him, its voice a tinny scrape from the square speaker housing. Sealed from every external network, the artificial intelligence could only observe and advise. "Dermal thickening is sufficient to withstand the Plateau's atmospheric conditions."
paragraphs.speaker: tinny

paragraphs: Dennis' gaze dropped to her nipples. Not even hard. As if the cold didn't exist for her.

paragraphs.text: "Quiet the passenger."
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs.text: "Applying the muffle," the CIX responded.
paragraphs.speaker: tinny

paragraphs: The amber cloud entered through the floor vent in a slow curl, thickening fast. It moved like a tide coming in around her ankles, then her calves. The soup of heavy isotopes and neurosedatives rose through the sub-zero air.
*Whirr. Ssssss.*
When the gas touched her skin, the gray surface buckled. Oily beads pushed up through the tectonic cracks of her thighs. Her head snapped back.
He couldn't hear her scream. The chamber was soundproofed. But he read her lips. She was calling his name.
She struggled against the gas like a drunken sailor. Her arms rose, elbows tucked in, fists swinging wildly at the chemical cloud that had no face to hit.

paragraphs.text: "Visitor resisting the agent," the CIX warned.
paragraphs.speaker: tinny

paragraphs: Reed's thumb found the PURGE toggle.
Envee threw herself against the glass.
*THUNK.*
The milkiness in her eyes fractured. The fog peeled it back into a piercing blue. A human iris.

She dropped to her knees. Her back arched until the vertebrae groaned. Two jagged slivers broke through the gray skin between her shoulder blades. They were wet. Folded. Shivering with the delicacy of a newborn.
*Please,* her lips formed.
Dennis' thumb moved to another toggle.

The vents roared. Neurotoxins purged. The wings — if that's what they were — drew back into bloody slits. She crawled to the glass and peeled at the gray crust on her arm. Pink beneath it. Human skin. It lasted only a second before the cold forced the gray to scab over once more.

A figure in a Köldur thermal suit stepped through the steaming frame. He approached her without hurry. She offered no resistance. She surrendered to his arms. Her knees gave way, and she folded against him. He lifted her as though she weighed nothing, turned, and disappeared with her into the white mist.
Dennis watched the empty chamber as though she were still there. He didn't blink until his eyes burned.

The viviflux deck was a narrow gallery of brushed steel. Conduits snaked along every surface. No windows to the stars. The gallery connected four modules. To his right, a curve of polished chrome released jets of steam, obscuring the far end of the corridor.
*Hiss. Clunk.*
The pressure lock cycled.
The figure emerged through the steam wall. The Köldur suit dripped with decontaminant slurry. White vapor curled around the suit's bulk.
The man unsealed the visor and pulled it off. Damp, dark hair clung to his forehead. He was broad-shouldered, with a stubby beard. His eyes were bloodshot, yet they looked loyal.

paragraphs.text: "How is she, Perera?" Dennis asked. He worked the clasps along the suit's hip.
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs: Ian Perera wiped his forehead. His lungs labored.

paragraphs.text: "In shock. Still there." His voice was gravelly.
paragraphs.speaker: ian-perera

paragraphs.text: "Finally." Dennis produced a shim from his front pocket. The muffle needed the real thing.
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs: Ian eyed the shim.
Dennis handed it over.

paragraphs.text: "A shopping list. Essentials to continue our integration."
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs.text: "What. Milk and eggs?" Ian turned the shim. He inspected both sides.
paragraphs.speaker: ian-perera

paragraphs: A carbon-fiber sliver. As thin as a fingernail. Etched with a symbol picturing a dark center with eight sharp arms radiating outward like spikes. Like antlers. They caught the blue lab light and held it.

paragraphs.text: "We tried synthetic reagents," Dennis said. "Prisms. Scattershot. Every time, the guests found their way back. Found their way in. We need organic compounds. Neuropeptides. Pineal distillates. Spinal fluids. Stem cells. Fresh. That's why I'm sending you back."
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs.text: "Why me?"
paragraphs.speaker: ian-perera

paragraphs: Dennis gripped Ian's shoulder.

paragraphs.text: "Because you have skin in the game. There's someone you need to meet. Kaspar Savannen. Make sure he gets this. No one else."
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

paragraphs: Ian pocketed the shim.

paragraphs.text: "No one must know," Dennis said. "Not even your wife."
paragraphs.speaker: dennis-reed

sections.heading:
34 CLICKS POST-UNFOLDING 
 CAPTAIN'S QUARTERS · FNS DÁINN
paragraphs: Ionie pulled the wooden-covered slate from her lap. The dark glass beneath it bled text into the dim cabin. It was an entry she'd already read a dozen times.
*< LOG ENTRY: 4B-YREUS >*

*Reed has reached out for help. With the Fold gone, the crew of Yreus Station can no longer sustain themselves. They must now be provisioned by us. That means breaching quarantine if they are to survive.*

paragraphs.text: *Ionie, find a way to supply them without drawing attention. I know what I'm asking. Here's how to contact Reed.*

*When Yreus relays messages via the tightbeam, it always returns an acknowledgment. We've been communicating through these acks, hiding messages in them. Routing the acks through the transducer with the attached hash allows decryption. The same works in reverse.*
*Yreus, of course, isn't relaying anything anymore. But the protocol still functions. I've kept the line alive under the pretense of checking for restoration, ponging regularly.*
*Use it. Carefully.*

paragraphs: The text bled back to black. Ben's logs included classified blueprints of the station. The revelation that Yreus had been manned came as a shock. Moving back and forth through the Fold. It was a direct violation of the fleet charter's containment protocol. The Fold was a one-way street. A safety measure.
*Ttap. Ttap. Ttap.*
Ionie's nail clicked against her front tooth.

paragraphs.text: *But how can I bring resources I don't have to a station that isn't supposed to be manned, and do so without drawing eyes? With my own ship chained to anchor, waiting to be scrapped? Does Ben really understand what he was asking me to do? Impossible.*
And then she picked up Ben's voice in her thoughts. *Make the impossible possible.*

paragraphs: Ben had taught her inversion. Think in the opposite direction.
She couldn't take resources from Mairee to the station.
She leaned back. The chair's recycled leather groaned. *Crr-eak.*

paragraphs.text: *Could I haul the station?* The thought hooked into her brain. A torn nail dropped from her mouth.

paragraphs: A chime announced the comms link. *Pong.*
Eva Bellamy's face bled into view on the holoscreen. Her left eyelid twitched.

paragraphs.text: "Captain Jia," Bellamy said. "The skimmers are reporting differences in the fuel manifests. Discrepancies."
paragraphs.speaker: eva-bellamy

paragraphs: Ionie leaned forward.

paragraphs.text: "I will not sunset the Dáinn. Decommissioning her is a mistake. The skimmers weren't drawing fuel. We bypassed them."
paragraphs.speaker: ionie-jia

paragraphs: She waited for the explosion, but Bellamy's face remained a mask save for the twitch.

paragraphs.text: "I've been reviewing the Yreus Array's true specifications."
paragraphs.speaker: ionie-jia

paragraphs.text: "Yreus?! It's a dead radio."
paragraphs.speaker: eva-bellamy

paragraphs.text: "The manifest lists it as an unmanned array. The blueprints tell a different story. It was an outpost. Manned. Scientists. Pioneers. It's been used as a refueling stop before. It's got labs. Life-support. Shielding. Lead lining. Gold contacts. Rare-earth composites. Even fuel. Worth the trip to salvage it."
paragraphs.speaker: ionie-jia

paragraphs: Bellamy's eye had stopped twitching. The tension left the controller's shoulders in a visible slump. Color returned to her cheeks.

paragraphs.text: "The Dáinn is yours," Bellamy said. Her gaze dropped to her terminal. "Wiggle it how you will. I won't interfere. And with whatever is going on below, I doubt Corbin will be in a position to stop you."
paragraphs.speaker: eva-bellamy

paragraphs: Bellamy's expression shifted to something hauntingly quiet right before the channel cut.

sections.heading: FREYA HOMESTEAD
paragraphs: Lysanne hitched Vilde higher against her shoulder. The muscle in her upper arm burned. The commander was lean, yet she pulled at Lysanne's joints like lead. Vilde's knees buckled every third step. Stasis had hollowed her. At the med-post, Lysanne had wrestled the woman into a medical officer's overalls. The fabric was stiff.

paragraphs.text: "Keep going," Vilde muttered into Lysanne's neck.
paragraphs.speaker: astrid-vilde

paragraphs: They moved through the old truss of the decommissioned flagship. Metal ribs arched above them like the skeleton of a prehistoric beast. A cool breeze rolled off the mountains, carrying the scent of wet stone and pine. The truss opened. The Central Corridor stretched ahead. On the ridge, turbines turned their blades with a slow, hypnotic lethargy. Between the antennas, the *Brisinger's* funeral pyre rose like a jagged new mountain of scorched alloy.
Vilde stopped. It nearly took them both down.

paragraphs.text: "That's not the harbor."
paragraphs.speaker: astrid-vilde

paragraphs: Lysanne tightened her grip on the commander's waist.

paragraphs.text: "It's the *Brisinger*, Commander. She fell."
paragraphs.speaker: lysanne-sutherland

paragraphs: Vilde's pupils dilated. Her eyes drank in the glare of the wreckage. Her gaze drifted to the amber Grid pipelines on their left.
*Phompf. Phompf.*

They continued. To their right, the Habs were stacked like a honeycomb. Behind the thick glass of one unit, a family pressed forward: parents and two children. Their hands were flat against the window.

paragraphs.text: "The Grid locked them in," Lysanne said.
paragraphs.speaker: lysanne-sutherland

paragraphs: Upon seeing Vilde's ghost, the settlers began a rhythmic, soundless banging. More faces appeared. More palms against glass. They hammered the windows. They kicked the doors. The sound didn't escape. The pipelines pumped faster in response.
*Phompf-phompf. Phompf-phompf.*
Three Eyewyn orbs drifted toward the junction.
*Whirr.*

Gimbals shifted. One orb dipped low, hovering inches from Vilde's face. The slackness of stasis vanished from the commander's features. Her jaw set. The softness drained from her eyes, replaced by a cold, operational clarity. Vilde pushed off Lysanne's shoulder. She stood on her own strength. The sudden shift in weight sent a jolt of vertigo through Lysanne.
FOX rose ahead in black angles, its dark walls housing the Freya colony's command center and Grid controls.
One Eyewyn stayed with them, watching over Lysanne's shoulder.

A guardian sat at the bottom of the entrance ramp. His head was down. As they neared, he looked up. He froze. His mouth opened, but the air failed him. They walked past. He followed them like a shroud.
The weighted doors remained shut. Then the magnetic locks disengaged.

paragraphs.text: The groan reverberated through the frame as the doors parted without a touch. Inside, the atmosphere shifted. The air was filtered. Fresh. Sterile. Dry enough to itch the back of the throat. The commander walked straight toward the central control room. Her gait was stiff but unbroken. Lysanne followed half a step behind. *The ghost is gone.*

paragraphs: Astrid Vilde entered the sanctum.

Lysanne had expected Ulre Corbin to be there — or, at the very least, someone to stop them from reaching the command center. Instead, the doors had opened without challenge. The operators stood halfway up from their stations. They hovered in a state of kinetic indecision. Screens surrounding them displayed a mosaic of disaster: crumbled cranes at the docks, the crashed bridge, the *Brisinger's* wreckage rewriting the horizon. One showed the Eyewyn feed.
One officer adjusted his collar. His fingers trembled. His eyes went wide.

paragraphs.text: "Commander," he whispered. "Welcome back."
paragraphs.speaker: fox-operator

paragraphs: Astrid stepped forward.

paragraphs.text: "Open the habs. All of them."
paragraphs.speaker: astrid-vilde

paragraphs: A mob formed near the plaza and the dome. A sea of gnashing teeth and frantic limbs. Angry. Elated. Terrified. Liberated.

Ulre Corbin did not move. He sat on a wooden bench in one of the garden beds far removed from the mob. His world had narrowed to a cluster of deep-purple alpine flowers. He traced the faint silver veins on the petals.
His collar was unhooked. The stiff fabric scratched at his neck. A smear of soot marked his left cuff: a gritty reminder of the disaster.
Above, the *Brisinger* drew another mountain in the skyline. It trailed a plume of orange fire into the purple sky.

A shadow fell over the flowerbed. He did not really register the young ensign, nor acknowledge her presence. But, even with only a glance, he noted she was soaked with sweat. Mascara smeared her cheeks in jagged dark tracks.

paragraphs.text: "Director," she gasped. "There's a rumor. Vilde. That she's back. People are gathering at the dome."
paragraphs.speaker: ensign

paragraphs.text: "Then why are you here?" Ulre asked. Not looking up.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: Without another word, she ran back toward the dome.
Ulre went back to studying the petals.
*Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen.*
The ego death he was experiencing was a slow, quiet hemorrhage. A draining of the self to make room for the other. Then something inside him buzzed.
*Bzzz-zzz. Bzzz-zzz.*
Agitated bees. A pressure behind his sternum. He inhaled. The purple of the flowers turned to a gray wash.

Someone else watched through his eyes. This thing had been searching, discovering emotions as they presented themselves like new colors blending into an existing spectrum. He had existed as a passenger. Until now. The hemorrhage made space. The guest seeped through.

paragraphs.text: *Am I—*

paragraphs: The thought was not yet fully formed, but it was there. Everything was loud. Unreasonably, overwhelmingly loud.
*Skreeeeee — krrr-tat-tat-tat.*

The body shifted. A shoulder tightened: a hard, involuntary knot. A hand flexed experimentally. The fingers felt long, clumsy, and distant. The legs were the next puzzle. Two pillars of bone and meat. Shivering.
He stood. The movement was jerky. He swayed like a mast in a storm.

paragraphs.text: "Stupid," he rasped.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: The voice was a shock. Like a gunshot in a library.
He took a step. His left boot didn't land where he had intended. It came down hard on the purple petals.
*Splat.*

paragraphs.text: "Sorry, little Colorsss," he murmured. The sibilance surprised him. He shook his head hard, as if dislodging water from his ears.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "Gaaargggh."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: The sound caught in his throat. It turned into a loud, wet snort. His sinuses felt clogged with someone else's contents. He squeezed the bridge of his nose and leaned forward.
*Hhk-tuh.*
He spat a glob of mucus onto the gravel between his boots. He wiped his lip with the back of his hand. Then he studied the hand itself: the liver spots, the fine hair.

paragraphs.text: "Yes, so this is what I have been dealing with."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: He rolled his shoulders like a boxer stepping into the ring. He took a few slow steps across the garden. His movements were not as shaky now. The tremors were fading. The host was yielding.
He gazed out at the carnage. The dust clouds. The fumes. He squinted against the glare.

paragraphs.text: "Æzal," he muttered. There was recognition in the tone. Irritation. "You dramatic little arsonist. What did you kindle this time?"
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: Then he smiled. Narrow. Slanted. Privately amused.

paragraphs.text: "Right," he said quietly. "Let's see."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: He began walking toward the wreck. Each step was more certain than the last. Behind him, the crushed alpine flowers trembled in the wind.
Ulre's legs were wobbly. But moving. Taking long strides.
He tried to form an intention. A command.

paragraphs.text: *Stop.*

paragraphs: The legs ignored him. Both of them.

He was mostly blind. Occasionally, a prickle of wind registered on the skin of his hands. It no longer felt like his. Then it vanished. Mostly, it was a numb, velvet darkness. He was falling through a well with no bottom.

paragraphs.text: *Tell me what you want,* he thought, trying to send a signal up.
*Stuff,* the thought replied. *From the wreck. Now shut up.*

paragraphs: Deeper now.

There. Way down. An entity watched him from the gloom. He couldn't hold its face. Every time Ulre focused, the features melted from old to young, from male to female, from human to reptilian. He gave up trying to fix the image.

paragraphs.text: "You've been here before," the entity said.
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "No."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "You've been somewhere like here. Many times."
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "Have I?"
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "Yes," the figure said. "The waiting."
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "I hate waiting."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "Yes. You do."
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "What are you?"
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: The face shifted at his visual periphery. It became a cluster of shifting polygons. "You know what I am," it said.
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "I don't."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "When you learned that certain parts of yourself were not safe. You sent them here. One at a time. You were very thorough."
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "I survived," Ulre said.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "No."
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs.text: "My body. Someone's wearing it."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: "Like you were wearing mine."
paragraphs.speaker: urael

paragraphs: The one above them slowed to a stop. The deceleration traveled all the way down. The wind came again. Bitter and sharp.
The phantom hands were holding something. Cold. Latched. Metal.
He fumbled the crate. The latches were intact. The casing showed impact damage on one corner. He opened it.
*Sss-creak.*

He dove half into the crate, rummaging through surveying instruments. He held up various items one at a time, turning them in the weak light. Brass. Glass. Plastic. Then he found a kit bag, half-buried under a surveyor's tripod. He pulled it out. The bag was a crew duffel made of heavy canvas. He unzipped it and shook out the contents: standard-issue stretchy bamboo clothes and a wash kit.

paragraphs.text: "Yesss," he said softly.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: He continued scavenging. Certain sections of the *Brisinger* had compressed. Some had collapsed entirely into mangled ribs of steel. He found a small galley with the fixtures still bolted in place. A cabinet hung open like a broken jaw. Packages of rations lay scattered across the deck. He opened a pack. Orange powder. He tasted it.
*Wooff.*
Citrus stung his tongue. He put six of the powders in his pack. He paused in the middle of the galley, glancing up at the ceiling, then at the walls, and finally down at the deck.
*Hm.*
He hadn't thought about shelter. He was thinking about it now.

He continued scavenging. He entered a crew bunk. A single cot. A personal locker had been forced partly open by the impact. A fold-down desk with a magnetic surface held a set of cards bound by a rubber band. He pulled one card out. Hand-illustrated. The image was a tower. Lightning-struck. Figures falling from its windows. The crown was blown clean off. He rotated it. Then he rotated it again. The tower rose upward just as convincingly as it hung down. The card didn't care which way it was held. The tower held no allegiance to gravity.

He held another. A figure hung by one foot from a wooden beam. Arms relaxed. A calm expression on its face. He rotated this one too. Hanging by the foot or hanging by the neck. The face remained the same. Unbothered. At peace with both interpretations.

paragraphs.text: "Fun," he said. He placed the deck in a small compartment in his bag.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: He found a box with dice. Eight shapes made of stone, bone, a nameless translucent material, and something shadowy and heavy. He rolled one across the desk.
*Clack.*
It landed on seven. He picked it up and examined the facets.

paragraphs.text: "Luck," he said. He tucked the dice away.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: On the locker shelf sat a growing kit with a sealed tray and six foil seed envelopes. Each label was written in a script so small he had to hold it to his borrowed eyes to read. Basil. Cress. Something crossed out. Marigold. Fennel. A seventh envelope was labeled *Magic*. It was thicker than the others, the foil carefully resealed with adhesive tape. He smelled the envelope. Through the foil came a scent of deep earth, old wood, and something sour underneath.

paragraphs.text: "Magic?" he wondered. Curious, he took them.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: A small framed picture lay on the floor. Its glass was a spiderweb of cracks. Three people stood along a dock, squinting in a sun that was now millions of miles away. One held up a fish.
He studied the faces. Then he put it back on the slanted shelf.

He crouched by the cot. Underneath it, he found a pair of worn boots, a rolled-up exercise mat, and a sealed box. He strapped the mat to his pack. He opened the box and found letters on real paper and a child's drawing that could have been a ship or a fish. It also contained a lock of hair wrapped in foil.
Then he flipped the mattress. An object rested against the bed frame. Smooth. It fit perfectly in his hand. He pressed the single button.
*Bzzz-vvvvvv.*
He threw it in surprise. It skidded across the desk and struck the wall.
*Grrrttt. Grrrttt.*

paragraphs.text: "Ah," he said, staring at the vibrating thing. He picked it up and turned it off. He turned around and then turned back.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs.text: *Fine.*

paragraphs: He granted it a place in the bag. He lifted the duffel over one shoulder. Judged the weight. Tried the other shoulder.

paragraphs.text: "Right."
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: He stepped over debris and ducked under fallen beams. He needed a place. Not just tonight. He stopped in the shadow of a collapsed section of the *Brisinger's* aft hull and listened. He set the bag down quietly.

There were Humans working in the open ground beyond the crash site. They were constructing something. The walls rose in curves that leaned inward without meeting. The materials were a hybrid — sections of stripped hull plating interwoven with something living. Branches, he thought at first. Then he saw the pulsing white threads. The mycelia. The network in the soil had been coaxed upward, woven into the walls.

He watched the Humans. One's head sat at a slightly different angle on the neck. Another stood with shoulders drawn back. Another trailed the site, and the network brightened in a slow bioluminescent wave following its passage.

paragraphs.text: *Æzal. Very impressive. Very — you.*

paragraphs: With the thought, his own name reverberated through the stolen marrow of his bones.

paragraphs.text: *Uræl. Little brother. Is that you?*

paragraphs: He needed distance. Quickly. He'd poked his nose where he shouldn't have. If he touched the mycelia, Æzal would feel him. Fight for control of the body.

paragraphs.text: *Uræl. Yes. That's right. That's me. A long time ago.*

paragraphs: Uræl half-carried, half-dragged the bag through the *Brisinger's* shadow. North. Up the ridge. Halfway up, he located a narrow shelf in the rock face. It was deep enough to be out of the wind. An overhang formed a natural roof to keep the sky out. He stepped onto the ledge.

paragraphs.text: "Home," he said.
paragraphs.speaker: ulre-corbin

paragraphs: Even the wreck was invisible from here. He pulled a ration pack from his bag. The orange powder almost choked him. He leaned against the rock wall, waiting for the coughing to stop. His eyes watered. Then burned. He needed a pulse to recompose himself.
Then he unstrapped the mat. His body was a leaden weight now. A pressure rose through him like water finding its level until he lost sense of all his limbs.
He fell. Down the well.
Deep.
